headline: Flagship LLM costing 5.8x more lost in niche production app benchmark
summary: A developer's custom benchmark for a BaZi chart app found that the most expensive LLM was outperformed by a model costing significantly less, highlighting the need for domain-specific evaluation.
details: A developer building an app for personalized BaZi (Chinese Four Pillars) birth chart readings benchmarked 8 LLMs on their specific workload. The goal was to find cost-effective and accurate models for a niche domain full of trap terminology.

The results revealed that the most expensive flagship model performed worse than a model costing 5.8 times less. This finding underscores that generic LLM benchmarks are often insufficient for specialized production applications.

The evaluation led to a two-tier model strategy: a cheap and accurate small model for the free tier, and a mid-tier model for paid users. A surprising discovery was that the mid-tier's previous generation offered equal accuracy at a lower cost, serving as an ideal fallback.

The app implements a robust routing layer with ordered fallback chains. Each route specifies a provider, endpoint, model, and list price. This ensures that if the primary workhorse model fails, a backup can serve the request.

Crucially, the system differentiates between transient rate-limit throttling and permanent quota exhaustion for 429 errors. Retrying the same model for quota issues is a waste of time; the system must skip to the next route, a distinction learned by analyzing provider-specific error taxonomies.

To prevent persistent issues, the app never caches fallback stubs. If a reading fails, it returns placeholder text with an `ok: false` flag, preventing the placeholder from being saved to the database and ensuring the system retries on the next request.

Each business action (a reading, involving up to 7 parallel calls) emits a usage event, with costs computed against the model that actually served it. This provides precise cost tracking, showing approximately $0.0021 per paid-tier call and $0.0005 per free-tier call.

The app, auspiceoracle.com, is a bilingual BaZi calculator where a deterministic engine computes the chart, and the LLM is strictly constrained to phrasing the results, a design choice that will be detailed in a future article.

headline_marked: [[Attest: ADK agent audits models on SEC advisers]] for compliance and accuracy
headline: Attest: ADK agent audits models on SEC advisers for compliance and accuracy
summary: Attest is an ADK agent designed to audit what other AI models say about SEC-registered advisers, scoring their responses against official Form ADV filings to ensure accuracy and provide an immutable record.
details: Attest is an ADK agent built to address the challenge of unrecorded AI descriptions of businesses, particularly for SEC-registered investment advisers. The SEC's 2026 examination priorities highlight AI, focusing on firms' claims about their own AI, but not what other models say about them.

The agent runs a fixed battery of factual questions about SEC-registered advisers on a schedule. It scores each AI-generated answer against the firm's official Form ADV Part 1A filing and appends the result to a hash-chained archive.

The system is orchestrated by Cloud Scheduler, which triggers monthly jobs via Pub/Sub to an agent running on Cloud Run. This agent utilizes six distinct tools: two for reading ground truth, one for scoring, one for appending evidence, and two for managing per-firm memory.

The archive is designed to be append-only, ensuring immutability with hash-chained entries, sequence numbers, timestamps, and model IDs. This chain tail advances within a Firestore transaction, with payloads stored in Cloud Storage, preventing replays from overwriting existing entries.

Attest is built on the Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) and leverages three different Gemini models. Gemini-3.5-flash-lite handles orchestration and subject model tasks, while Gemini-3.1-flash-lite is used for scoring to maintain comparability with pre-build experiments.

A notable development challenge involved integrating Google's Model Armor, which initially failed due to a 403 PERMISSION_DENIED error. This was traced to using a global API host instead of the required per-region host, highlighting a critical detail for API interactions.
